places.name: Oiran-douchuu procession
places.note: High-clogged oiran gliding down the main street with attendants — free with admission and the best photo of the day. Check the gate timetable.

places.name: Ninja Karakuri Mansion
places.note: Tilted floors and hidden doors — pair it with the Ninja Trick Maze; together they fit a 2.5-hour slot alongside two shows.

places.name: Mizugei-za water-magic show
places.note: One of the three shows worth choosing between; grab the printed timetable at the gate the moment you enter.

places.name: Minami-machi Bugyosho
places.note: Courtroom comedy — the most accessible of the shows if nobody in the group reads Japanese.

places.name: Kamado-ya (dango)
places.note: ¥300–1,400. Between shows, the dango here is one of the only things you can eat standing.

places.name: Nihon-soba Yabu
places.note: ¥900–1,700 — the sit-down option if you would rather eat than see a third show.

places.name: H-II rocket, Expo Center forecourt
places.note: A full-size 50 m rocket, floodlit, unfenced from the public path and needing no ticket — the best photo in walking distance.

places.name: Ibaraki natto
places.note: Ibaraki is Japan's natto capital — put it on tomorrow's breakfast plate, because the group will not meet it again.

places.name: Tsukuba Chuo Park
places.note: Unenclosed, no gate, so it works at 06:30 — pond, modernist civic buildings, and haze permitting Mount Tsukuba's twin peaks.

places.name: Miharashi Hill summit path
places.note: Green kochia domes with the Pacific behind. Shoot east from the summit, then low into the sun for translucent lime-green.

places.name: Seaside Train
places.note: ¥600 one-day ticket. With one hour and 215 hectares you cannot walk it, so this is not optional.

places.name: Ferris wheel
places.note: The only way to get the whole hill and the ocean in one shot inside a one-hour stop.

places.name: Hoshi-imo soft-serve, West Gate
places.note: Hitachinaka and neighbouring Tokai produce most of Japan's dried sweet potato, so this is genuinely local, not generic.

x.nameJp: 干しいもソフトクリーム

places.name: Glass House café
places.note: Out in the dune area — the one place to sit with a full Pacific horizon.

places.name: Toki no Kane bell tower
places.note: Three tiers, about 16 m, rebuilt 1894 after the Great Kawagoe Fire. Chimes 06:00 / 12:00 / 15:00 / 18:00 — you leave at 14:30, so it is a photo.

places.name: Kasho Umon imo-koi
places.note: Eaten hot at the Toki no Kane shop: a yam-flour steamed bun around Kawagoe sweet potato and chestnut-azuki paste. The most Kawagoe thing you can hold.

places.name: Ogakiku (unagi)
places.note: Founded 1807, in Nakacho. Commonly closed Mondays — today is Sunday, so it should be open, but an hour makes it a stretch.

places.name: Koedo Kurari — COEDO Beniaka
places.note: The beer actually brewed with Kawagoe sweet potato — a former sake brewery turned market hall.

places.name: Osawa House
places.note: 1792, the oldest kurazukuri on the street and a National Important Cultural Property.

places.name: Kawagoe Matsuri Kaikan
places.note: Apr–Sep 09:30–18:30, ¥300 or ¥240 for groups of 20+. Two real festival floats indoors — the one paid stop worth an hour.

places.name: Hachiko Statue
places.note: The group photo everyone expects. The queue thins noticeably after 22:30.

places.name: Scramble Square 2F walkway
places.note: Free, and the crossing only reads as a spectacle from height — from street level it is just a crowd.

places.name: Myth of Tomorrow mural
places.note: Taro Okamoto's enormous mural in the JR-to-Keio Inokashira passage — a genuinely major artwork most visitors walk straight past.

places.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Government South Observatory
places.note: FREE, 45F at 202 m, to 22:00 (last entry 21:30). Two Oedo Line stops for ¥180 — better than any paid tower, and both decks open on a Sunday.

places.note: About 1,300 seats, nine regional stalls, kiosk-fixed prices, no seating charge, effectively round the clock — the only place here that absorbs 35 people.

places.name: 13F rooftop bar & terrace
places.note: 62 open-air seats over the Kabukicho neon. Sunday hours are 14:00–22:30, not the 04:00 close it keeps midweek — go before 21:00.

places.name: Godzilla Head
places.note: The 12 m head above Hotel Gracery, free from the street. It roars on the hour to 20:00 — leave by 19:45 for the last one.

places.name: Hanazono Shrine
places.note: The only ungated patch of gravel, trees and lanterns in Kabukicho, six minutes away — the best dawn walk tomorrow, with a back exit into Golden Gai.

places.name: Golden Gai
places.note: Over 200 bars, most seating 5–10, so groups of four+ get turned away. Confirm the seat charge before sitting: usually ¥300–1,000, but not always.

places.name: Skywalk Window glass floor
places.note: Main Deck 1F: stand on glass and look 145 m straight down. Do it first — it jams the moment tour traffic arrives.

places.note: Main Deck 2F, the highest shrine in Tokyo's 23 wards — goshuin ¥300 and omamori ¥700, both deck-exclusive.

places.name: Zojoji Daiden courtyard
places.note: THE exterior group photo, 300 m away: main hall in front, tower behind, sun SE at 43° behind the photographer at 09:10. Frame the Daiden — the Sangedatsumon is in a restoration shed until about 2032.

places.note: Opens 09:00 and the soft serve is halal-certified — the one named early option, since the food court does not open until 11:00.

places.note: Skytree lies NNE, so at 09:40 with the sun SE it is front-lit and clean. Do not promise Fuji: Tokyo averages 2.9 visible days in September.

places.name: Namiyoke Inari Shrine
places.note: The market's guardian shrine — giant lion heads, and memorial stones to tamago, sushi and prawns. Start here and work back.

places.name: Tsukiji Yamacho (tamagoyaki)
places.note: 06:00–15:30, open 365 days — hot tamagoyaki on a skewer at about ¥150, and the one shop guaranteed open whatever the calendar says.

places.name: Marutake (tamagoyaki)
places.note: 04:00–14:30, Monday-open — the other big tamagoyaki name, run by the family of a well-known TV comedian.

places.name: Kitsuneya (hormone-don)
places.note: 06:30–13:30, ¥1,000–1,200, eaten standing at a plank counter. The most photographed queue in the market.

places.name: Tsukiji Sanokiya
places.note: 07:00–15:00, about ¥250 — the tuna-shaped 'maru' and 'honmaguro' cakes, and the easiest thing to hand round 35 people.

places.name: Sushizanmai Honten
places.note: Open 24 hours and the only place here that seats a group. Note Sushi Dai and Daiwa Sushi both moved to Toyosu in 2018.

places.name: Turret Coffee
places.note: Named for the turret trucks still nosing through the lanes, with one parked inside — the market's signature machine, standing still.

places.name: Information Center
places.note: Collect the floor map here and split 2.5 hours into two 70-minute halves with one hard regroup point. 220 units is too many to browse.

places.note: Chiba is peanut country and the boiled new crop is only sold roughly August to October — genuinely in season right now.

places.note: 100 m away in a converted Delta flight-catering factory: Edo-townscape build, open-air baths, stone-bed sauna. FREE to guests on a ¥1,800 voucher. Mondays 17:00–22:00 only.

places.name: California Restaurant
places.note: 1F, 140 seats. Its Hawaiian Buffet runs 1 July to 30 September, so mid-September is inside it.

places.note: 06:00–23:00, free, THREE free large-coach bays: a hill at the northern threshold of Runway A where landing aircraft pass low overhead.

places.name: 5F observation deck
places.note: Free, straight down Runway A, and the only place in the building where 35 people can spread out for a last group shot.

places.note: A last bowl of ramen or a conveyor sushi counter, plus bento for the gate. Before 07:30 only the 5F gachapon shop and the vending machines are trading.

places.name: THE ROOFTOP, Hotel Metropolitan Haneda
places.note: The zero-risk option whatever time you get in: a rooftop deck reached by the guest lift, taking in Terminal 3 and the runways, Tokyo Skytree, Tokyo Tower and the Rainbow Bridge, with a vending machine but no bar staff.

places.note: A 675 m bridge opened in 2022 linking Haneda to Kawasaki, with Mt Fuji up the Tama river on a clear morning and aircraft climbing overhead — 15–20 minutes each way, so realistic for keen early risers rather than all 35 before an 08:30 departure.

places.name: Taki-no-Yu public bath
places.note: Naruko Onsen Shrine's thousand-year-old sacred bath: two Aomori-cypress tubs per side at 44–46°C and 39–41°C, acidic pH 2.9 sulphur water — no showers, no taps, and no soap or shampoo sold, so bring your own from the hotel.

places.name: Waseda Sajiki-yu public bath
places.note: A concrete-terraced modern bathhouse over the spring that Waseda University engineering students drilled in 1948 — the latest-closing bath in town if dinner runs long.

places.name: Poppo no Ashiyu footbath
places.note: Two triangular cypress footbaths set about ten metres outside the ticket gate of JR Naruko Onsen Station. Nothing is provided, so carry a towel.

places.name: Yumeguri Hiroba footbath (Shimo-jigoku source)
places.note: A second free footbath in the car park beside the station, on a different source from Poppo about 50 m away — this is where the dawn steam-stroll starts.

places.name: Naruko Onsen Shrine
places.note: Founded in 835, reached by the stone stairway starting at Taki-no-Yu's entrance, with the hall's bell wrapped against the sulphur. Best free vantage back down over the tin roofs of the bath town.

x.hoursText: Grounds open at all hours, free; goshuin during staffed daytime hours only

places.name: Mochidokoro Fukase
places.note: Kuri-dango — a whole syrup-steeped chestnut inside mochi under sweet walnut-miso sauce, ¥400 for two, the same recipe for over a century. Opens 09:00, so it is a stretch against an 08:30 coach: ask the guide to stop.

places.name: Sakurai Kokeshi-ten honten
places.note: The workshop is behind the counter, three minutes from the station — Naruko kokeshi are the ones that squeak when you turn the head. Opens too late for the 08:30 coach, so it is a lunchtime-detour ask, not a dawn stop.

places.name: Tennoji Anabara-yu public bathhouse
places.note: Anabara's ONLY public bath and the one thing you can walk to — about 230 m, three or four minutes east along the road. Bring ¥400 in coins and your own towel, wash before entering, and warn the group the water is genuinely hot. Open Thursday evening AND from 06:00 on the Friday.

places.name: Yoshikawaya riverside baths & book lounge
places.note: The honest answer for Anabara: the hotel IS the evening. Two open-air baths over the Surikami rapids, a footbath, and a lounge with 4,000 manga titles open to 23:00 — enough for 19:30–22:30 without anyone leaving the building, and a good option for whoever will not undress in a public bath.

places.name: Sabako-yu — the historic wooden bathhouse
places.note: Iizaka's icon, long known as Japan's oldest wooden public bathhouse building — caption it accurately, because today's hut is a faithful 1993 rebuild in the Meiji form. It stands in its own square with Sabako Shrine and is lit at night, so it photographs beautifully even if nobody bathes. Five minutes by taxi; the hotel shuttle does not run after 18:00.

x.hoursText: 06:00–21:00, last entry 20:40 · closed Mondays · ¥400 adult / ¥200 child

places.name: Kyu-Horikiri-tei — free hand bath and footbath
places.note: The best free evening stop in Iizaka and open until 21:00, which almost nothing else is. A restored merchant estate with a big storehouse, plus an outdoor hand bath and footbath that suit 35 people far better than a tiny public bath — everyone sits, nobody undresses, and Iizaka kokeshi are displayed inside. 90 m from Sabako-yu, so pair them.

x.hoursText: 09:00–21:00, essentially no closing days · admission FREE

places.name: Totsuna-bashi bridge (floodlit)
places.note: The photograph of Iizaka: a 51.7 m steel arch bridge of 1915, one of the oldest surviving Taisho arch bridges and a Japan Society of Civil Engineers heritage site, spanning the Surikami gorge by the station. Free, works in rain, and the Harai-yu bath sits at its foot so one stop covers both.

x.hoursText: 24 hours, free · railings and arch floodlit nightly since 2009

places.name: Harai-yu public bathhouse
places.note: The right first public bath for anyone who has never done this: rebuilt in 2011, the newest and largest of the eight, and crucially it has BOTH a hot and a warm tub. Iizaka's springs arrive at 50–70°C and Sabako-yu in particular defeats most first-timers.

x.hoursText: 06:00–21:00, last entry 20:40 · closed Tuesdays · ¥500 adult / ¥250 child

places.name: Gyoza no Terui, Iizaka branch
places.note: Fukushima City's signature dish, enban gyoza — a whole pan-shaped disc of gyoza flipped out onto the plate — and Terui is the name most associated with it. Open on the Thursday, but it is a taxi each way after an 18:00 kaiseki, so this is for whoever skips dessert.

x.hoursText: 17:00–21:00 or until sold out · closed Wednesdays · one disc (22 gyoza) ¥1,200

places.name: Fureai Bridge
places.note: Ninety metres from the hotel — essentially its front garden. A pedestrian-only plaza bridge with a nationally rare Vierendeel truss, giant oni murals on the stair walls and the Kinuta mascot statues, lit at night. It is also the outdoor fallback for the yukata reel, though taking 35 borrowed yukata onto a public bridge needs the hotel's say-so.

places.name: Premium Lounge, in the lobby
places.note: Listed because Kinugawa closes early and this is where 35 people will actually end up: free coffee, soft drinks and alcohol, a cool-down area, a big manga corner, free table tennis in yukata. It is the SAME room as the yukata rack and the group photo, so time the shoot against lounge traffic.

places.name: Kurogane Bridge
places.note: The town's symbol bridge, originally built in 1910 to haul materials for a hydro-electric scheme and then the pivot of the resort's growth — bronze sculptures on the parapets and the best in-town look down the gorge. About eight minutes on foot.

x.hoursText: 24 hours, free

places.name: Takimi Bridge — the abandoned-hotel viewpoint
places.note: The one viewpoint for Kinugawa's much-photographed riverside ruins, and the resort's only suspension bridge. From here you see five derelict hotels stacked on the east cliff — including this hotel's own east annexe, closed in 2008. The park beside it has toilets and a coach bay, so it also works as a ten-minute stop on the way out.

x.hoursText: 24 hours, free — but the deck is wooden, unlit and sways, so dawn or daylight only

places.name: Kinuko-no-yu free footbath
places.note: A free footbath under the right-bank end of Kurogane Bridge, paired with the Kinuta and Kinuko oni mascots. Listed honestly: on this itinerary you cannot reach it, so do not promise it — it only works if the group gets free time before 17:00.

x.hoursText: 09:00–17:00, FREE — shut before you arrive at 18:20 and shut again before the 08:30 coach

places.name: Kinu Tateiwa Great Suspension Bridge
places.note: A 140 m pedestrian suspension bridge hung 40 m above the Kinugawa, nicknamed the matchmaking bridge, with the 100 m Tateiwa rock beside it and a viewing deck ten minutes further up. Twenty-two minutes on foot — a good Saturday dawn option for the keen walkers, too far for the whole group.

x.hoursText: 24 hours, free, no gate — unlit and reached by steps, so dawn or daylight only

places.name: Kinugawa Onsen Station plaza
places.note: Fourteen minutes on foot: the free footbath (shut by the time you arrive), the Kinuta oni statue, the resort's shops, and the turntable beside platform 1 where the SL Taiju steam locomotive is physically turned around. An evening stroll for the shops and the turntable rather than a soak.

places.name: Tsukuba Expo Center — H-II rocket forecourt

You need no ticket to see or photograph it — the ¥500 buys the museum, long shut by 18:30. A 600 m walk, 30–40 minutes round trip.

x.suggestionPhoto: Only two frames today: the 07:00 assembly at the Penang check-in counter, and whatever anyone shoots from THE ROOFTOP at midnight. For the assembly, plain solid colours over busy prints — a 35-person line-up in patterns turns to visual noise at any distance. Note Trip 12 does NOT shoot the airport reel; that is Trips 1–10, so this is a casual record shot, not a mission.
x.suggestionPractical: Twenty hours and twenty minutes door to door in a cabin held near 23°C, so a light long-sleeve layer beats a jacket you have to carry. Slip-on shoes for two security screenings. Malaysia to Japan is a 1-hour time change only, so no real jet lag — but you reach the room close to midnight and the coach leaves at 08:30.

x.suggestionPhoto: The Matsushima palette is blue-grey sea, near-black pine islets and VERMILION bridges. That makes two colours risky: dark green disappears into the pines, and orange or red fights the vermilion of the Fukuura and Godaido bridges, which is the one colour every photo here is built around. Mid-tone blue, navy or a soft neutral reads cleanly against both sea and pine. White works against the dark islets but blows out under a 49° sun at 13:18.
x.suggestionPractical: Matsushima is 29°/22° and coastal, so a sea breeze makes it feel kinder than inland — until 16:00, when the open 2F cruise deck is genuinely windy and carries spray. The three afternoon stops are 450 m, 500 m and 280 m apart on flat paving, so this is an easy walking day. The exception is Godaido: its two bridges have lattice floors that show the sea five metres below through the gaps, so no heels and no open-toe, and they cannot take a wheelchair.

x.suggestionPhoto: TODAY IS THE SUB-GROUP BANNER PHOTO, so this matters more than any other day. September Ginzan is a wall of deep green foliage, weathered dark-brown timber and a grey-green river — which means GREEN, BEIGE, BROWN AND OLIVE all disappear into the background. What lifts off it: white, cream, pale blue, and any clear mid-tone. Coordinate one thing with the photographer: the front row should not match the banner, or the banner stops reading. Because the sun runs down the street axis, shooting UP-street is straight into it — shoot down-street at 09:30–09:45 while the sun is lowest, or use fill flash.
x.suggestionPractical: Ginzan's 400 m street is car-free and flat, with a five-minute path on to Shirogane Falls that stays damp. Zao Fox Village is the day's real constraint: gravel and dirt on a slope, foxes roaming loose, and a rule set that is actually enforced — keep walking, never crouch or sit to fox level, no food or drink in your hands, and remove everything that dangles. Long trousers and closed shoes. September is moulting season, so the animals are patchy and the smell is strong in the heat; it gets into fabric.

x.suggestionPhoto: TWO MISSIONS TODAY, and they want opposite things. Tsuruga Castle is white plaster, GREY stone and a RED tiled roof over a green lawn: red and maroon clash with the roof, and dark green sinks into the lawn, so white, cream, navy and pale blue are the safe picks — and light clothing genuinely helps, because from the Honmaru the keep is back-lit with the sun behind it at 220°. Shoot from the SOUTH-EAST corner looking WNW rather than from due east, take it at 13:15–13:35 rather than 14:20, and expose for faces with fill flash. The evening yukata photo needs nothing from your wardrobe — the hotel provides the yukata — but wear something you can change out of in five minutes.
x.suggestionPractical: Goshikinuma at 820 m is the coolest stop, 22–25°C, but humid, with muddy boardwalk after rain and mosquitoes and horseflies still active in September. Then the Aizu basin: 28–30°C at about 79% humidity, and the Honmaru lawn is almost entirely unshaded — fill water bottles before the photo. Ouchi-juku is unshaded gravel, and the Miharashidai lookout is a genuine 20–25 minute round trip up steps that get slippery.

x.suggestionPhoto: Toshogu is the hard one on this trip: gilded gold and vermilion carving in deep cedar shade, punched through by hard sunlit gaps at a 56° sun. That is a brutal dynamic range, and it punishes both extremes — white blows out in the lit patches, black dies in the shade. Wear a MID-TONE. Kegon is the opposite and the one place all week where warm colours win: grey rock, white water, green cliff, so rust, mustard or coral genuinely pop. At Edo Wonderland everyone around you is in Edo costume, so either rent one or wear plain solids; modern prints look wrong in every frame.
x.suggestionPractical: The 09:20 Kegon stop is the single coolest hour of the trip — 1,269 m, roughly 17–19°C, with spray carrying about 150 m to the deck on a windy day, so a light layer AND the expectation of getting slightly damp. Toshogu is gravel and stone with 207 optional steps to the Okumiya; shoes stay on for the main route. Edo Wonderland is 49.5 hectares of gravel and timber, and costume rental takes 30–45 minutes to dress, which costs you a show.

x.suggestionPhoto: The single best colour day of the trip, and it has one hard rule: DO NOT WEAR GREEN AT HITACHI. Miharashi Hill in September is tens of thousands of lime-green kochia domes under a blue sky with the Pacific behind — anything green makes you part of the shrubbery. White, cream, coral, red and yellow are spectacular against it. Kawagoe inverts the rule: the kurazukuri warehouses are BLACK-plastered clay, so black and charcoal vanish into the walls, and light colours pop hard. Shibuya at 15:45 is mixed LED colour, where plain solids beat busy patterns.
x.suggestionPractical: Hitachi is the exposed bit: 215 hectares with no shade on a Pacific coast, strong sun at 48° and enough wind to take a hat off the back of your head. Then Kawagoe at 13:45 is the hottest hour of the whole trip — 30–31°C inland, on a treeless asphalt corridor with no shade at all. Between them is a 150 km, two-hour coach leg, and after Kawagoe another hour, so wear something you can sit in comfortably for three hours.

x.suggestionPhoto: Tokyo Tower is INTERNATIONAL ORANGE and white, and that dictates the day: orange and red clothing fights the tower in every frame. White, navy, denim blue and black all read cleanly against the orange lattice and a September sky. Tsukiji is the opposite problem — its lanes are roofed in blue and green tarpaulin, which throws a cold cast over skin, so a warm-toned top quietly cancels it. If you want one exterior group photo of the whole trip that looks composed, the Zojoji courtyard at 09:10 is it.
x.suggestionPractical: Tsukiji is the shoe decision: wet, fishy ground, narrow lanes, almost no seating, and stand-and-eat throughout — closed shoes you do not mind, and a small bag rather than a backpack you will swing into someone's display. Tokyo Tower's Main Deck has a glass floor you stand on, which is worth knowing if you are in a skirt. Shisui from 14:30 is flat, open-air and unshaded for two and a half hours.

x.suggestionPhoto: The last frames are the Terminal 1 group shot and whatever the 5F observation deck gives you. If the trip has a shirt or a company colour, today is the day to wear it — it is the one photo where 35 people are in one place, indoors, unhurried. Otherwise plain solids again.
x.suggestionPractical: Breakfast at 06:30 is the restaurant's opening minute and the coach follows, so lay everything out the night before. Then twenty hours home: slip-on shoes, a light long-sleeve for two cabins, and compression socks for 8h25 of seat time. Weigh bags before you leave the room — 25 kg checked, 7 kg hand-carry, one piece, nothing over 32 kg.
